units.source_excerpt: In order to impart some intuition about the model we begin by presenting a rigid body model. Next, we proceed to use our full model to reconcile various correct and incorrect claims about the sweet spot found in the literature. Finally, we discuss the sweet spot and performance of corked and aluminum bats, with a particular emphasis on hoop modes.
units.function: Preview a baseline-to-full-model progression and its applications.
units.reusable_pattern: We begin with {baseline} to expose {mechanism}, then use {full_model} to address {gap}, and finally apply it to {application}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use a progression when the models are unrelated.
Do not list model names without explaining the upgrade.

units.source_excerpt: We have encountered at least two notions of what the sweet spot should be defined as. We do not identify the two and focus exclusively on the second definition, which we now define more carefully.
units.function: Separate competing meanings before fixing the modeled construct.
units.reusable_pattern: We distinguish {construct} from {nearby_construct} and use {operational_definition} throughout this analysis.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not redefine the construct later without notice.
Do not infer excluded meanings in the conclusion.

units.source_excerpt: Our paper is organized as follows. First, we present the Brody rigid body model illuminating the recoil effects of impact. Next we present a full computational model based on wave propagation in a Euler-Bernoulli beam coupled with the ball modeled as a lossy spring.
units.function: Map the reader through the same model dependency order used by the analysis.
units.reusable_pattern: First, we use {baseline} to establish {mechanism}; next, we introduce {extension} to capture {omission}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not publish a roadmap that differs from the body order.

units.source_excerpt: We discuss these models not only to point out the confusion surrounding the sweet spot but also to highlight two basic issues in modeling the sweet spot. Our approach reconciles the tension between these different approaches while emphasizing the crucial role played by the time-scale of the collision.
units.function: Turn disagreements among prior models into a mechanism-specific research gap.
units.reusable_pattern: Prior models explain {known_effects} separately but leave {decision_gap}; we connect them through {bridge_mechanism}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim a gap without naming what prior models already accomplish.

units.source_excerpt: In this paper, we determine the sweet spot on a baseball bat.
units.function: State the paper's focal decision object directly.
units.reusable_pattern: We determine {decision object} for {system} under {operating conditions}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not leave the operating definition implicit.

units.source_excerpt: We capture the essential physics of the ball-bat impact by taking the ball to be a lossy spring and the bat to be an Euler-Bernoulli beam.
units.function: Compress the full model into two coupled physical abstractions.
units.reusable_pattern: Represent {subsystem_1} as {abstraction_1} and {subsystem_2} as {abstraction_2}, coupled through {interface}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call an abstraction essential without naming omissions.

units.source_excerpt: Our model allows for realistic bat geometries, rotation of the bat, and finite propagation speed of waves in the bat.
units.function: Name the mechanisms added beyond the rigid baseline.
units.reusable_pattern: The full model adds {geometry}, {motion}, and {finite-rate mechanism} to the baseline.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not list an extension that is absent from the equations.

units.source_excerpt: The status of baseball as the nation's pastime makes understanding the collision of an irregularly shaped slab of wood with a ball a compelling and interesting problem.
units.function: Move from domain relevance to the collision object.
units.reusable_pattern: In {domain}, understanding {interaction} requires modeling {irregular feature}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use cultural importance as technical evidence.

units.source_excerpt: Given a baseball bat and baseball, the final velocity of the ball is determined by the initial velocity and rotation of the ball, initial velocity and rotation of the bat, the relative orientation, and the point of impact.
units.function: Inventory the operating conditions that make the objective conditional.
units.reusable_pattern: Outcome {y} depends on {initial states}, {orientation}, and {decision variable}; fix the first terms before optimizing the last.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not report one universal optimum across changing conditions.

units.source_excerpt: Fixing the properties of the bat, ball, initial velocity of the ball, and angular velocity, we can now define the sweet spot as the location of the point of impact which maximizes the final velocity of the ball.
units.function: Give the speed-only operational objective and fixed conditions.
units.reusable_pattern: Holding {inputs} fixed, define {construct} as the {decision variable} that maximizes {response}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not merge this speed optimum with minimum hand discomfort.

units.source_excerpt: The simplest model predicts the sweet spot to be at the center of percussion. This model assumes that an impact location that minimizes discomfort to the hand also maximizes power transfer to the ball.
units.function: State the baseline prediction and the assumption that links two meanings.
units.reusable_pattern: Model {baseline} predicts {result} because it identifies {construct_1} with {construct_2} through {assumption}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not inherit the assumption after separating the constructs.

units.source_excerpt: Another model predicts the sweet spot to be between nodes of the two lowest natural frequencies of the bat.
units.function: Introduce the competing standing-wave account before testing collision duration.
units.reusable_pattern: An alternative account locates {construct} through {mechanism}; test whether its characteristic time and boundary conditions match the event.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not transfer free-vibration nodes directly to transient contact.

units.source_excerpt: Our main goal is to understand the sweet spot. A secondary goal is to understand the differences between the sweet spots of different bat types.
units.function: Separate the core mechanism goal from the material-comparison extension.
units.reusable_pattern: The primary goal is {mechanism question}; the secondary goal compares {design families} under the same metric.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not let the extension replace the core validation.

units.source_excerpt: We begin by only considering the rigid recoil effects of the bat-ball collision, much in the same way as Brody.
units.function: Declare the rigid baseline and the mechanism it isolates.
units.reusable_pattern: Begin with {baseline} to isolate {mechanism}, while deferring {omissions}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not present the baseline as the final model.

units.source_excerpt: Given our pre-collision conditions, we can write conservation of linear momentum, conservation of angular momentum, and the definition of the coefficient of restitution.
units.function: Build the baseline from three named physical laws.
units.reusable_pattern: Under {conditions}, combine {law_1}, {law_2}, and {closure relation} to solve {output}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not omit sign conventions.

units.source_excerpt: The figure also shows intuitively why the sweet spot is located somewhere between the center of mass and the end of the barrel.
units.function: Use opposing response components to explain an interior optimum.
units.reusable_pattern: As {decision} changes, {benefit} rises while {cost} falls; their combination produces an interior optimum.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not reverse the plotted direction in prose.

units.source_excerpt: However, this model tells only part of the story. Indeed some of our starting assumptions contradict each other.
units.function: Use an internal contradiction to motivate model escalation.
units.reusable_pattern: The baseline assumes {A} and {B}, but {time-scale or mechanism evidence} makes them incompatible; therefore add {extension}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not upgrade without naming the contradiction.

units.source_excerpt: We have attempted to combine the best features of previous models into our model.
units.function: Position the full model as a mechanism-preserving synthesis.
units.reusable_pattern: Retain {mechanism_1} from {model_1} and {mechanism_2} from {model_2}, then add {target-specific extension}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call incompatible equations a synthesis without an interface.

units.source_excerpt: To reiterate, the main features of our model are an emphasis on ball coupling with the bat, finite speed of wave propagation in short time-scale, and adaptation to realistic bats.
units.function: Restate the full model around three mechanism commitments before equations.
units.reusable_pattern: Before derivation, state that the model captures {interface}, {finite-rate process}, and {target geometry}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim a mechanism missing from the discretization.

units.source_excerpt: Our equations are a discretized version of the Euler-Bernoulli equations. The only force will be from the ball, which applies a force in the negative direction to the k-th segment.
units.function: Map the continuum beam to a local-force spatial discretization.
units.reusable_pattern: Discretize {continuum equation} on {grid}; apply {interface force} at {index} and state {boundary conditions}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not omit time step and convergence criteria.

units.source_excerpt: Let u(t) equal w(t) minus y_k(t). This variable will represent the compression of the ball, and we will replace F(t) with F(u(t),u'(t)).
units.function: Define the local contact coordinate that couples ball and beam.
units.reusable_pattern: Define relative state {u}={body position}-{interface displacement}; evaluate {force} from {u} and {rate}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not omit mass when converting force to acceleration.

units.source_excerpt: The maximum exit velocity in our example is around 26.7 m/s, and the sweet spot is 13 cm from the center of mass. Missing the sweet spot by up to 5 cm will only result in a 1 m/s difference.
units.function: Report optimum, location, tolerance, units, and scenario.
units.reusable_pattern: Under {scenario}, {response_max} occurs at {location}; deviations within {tolerance} change the response by at most {loss}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not transfer an illustrative baseline optimum to the full model.

units.source_excerpt: The force is zero after about 1.4 ms, while the effect of the collision reaches the distant part of the bat later.
units.function: Tie contact duration to causal propagation timing.
units.reusable_pattern: Signal {contact} ends at {time_1}, while {distant response} begins at {time_2}; compare these times to assess {mechanism}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer measured timing from simulation alone.

units.source_excerpt: For the base model the sweet spot is located at approximately 70 cm from the handle, farther out than predicted by the rigid body model.
units.function: Compare the full-model optimum with the baseline on one axis.
units.reusable_pattern: Under {base parameters}, the full model gives {x_star}, shifted {direction} from the baseline by {difference}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim accuracy from model disagreement alone.

units.source_excerpt: When we remove hysteresis the curves no longer cross, showing that the velocity-dependent energy loss in the ball produces the crossing.
units.function: Use an ablation to attribute a curve feature to one mechanism.
units.reusable_pattern: Removing {mechanism} eliminates {feature}; this supports attribution of {feature} to {mechanism} within the simulation.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call an internal ablation external validation.

units.source_excerpt: We vary the density, Young's modulus, handle shape, and initial ball velocity around the base bat parameters.
units.function: Declare the local parameter-sweep axes and base case.
units.reusable_pattern: Starting from {base case}, vary {parameters} one at a time over {ranges}, holding {inputs} fixed.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call one-factor sweeps global robustness.

units.source_excerpt: Lower density moves the optimum and changes the width of the high-performance region, while Young's modulus changes wave-return timing.
units.function: Interpret parameter trends through the wave mechanism.
units.reusable_pattern: Changing {parameter} shifts {output} because it changes {mechanism}; report range and reversal point.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer intentional design from a simulated trend.

units.source_excerpt: Changing the handle profile affects the response less than changing density or modulus in the tested cases.
units.function: Rank local sensitivity axes within the tested range.
units.reusable_pattern: Within {tested range}, {parameter_A} changes {metric} less than {parameter_B}; report the common scale used for comparison.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not rank effects across unmatched ranges.

units.source_excerpt: The initial ball speed changes both the input kinematics and the loss realized through the hysteretic contact law.
units.function: Separate direct input change from mechanism-mediated loss.
units.reusable_pattern: Parameter {p} affects {output} directly through {path_1} and indirectly through {path_2}; separate them with an ablation.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not attribute a compound effect to one path.

units.source_excerpt: We model a corked bat by hollowing the barrel and leaving wooden shells of 1 cm and 1.5 cm thickness.
units.function: State the structural surrogate and scenario dimensions before comparison.
units.reusable_pattern: Approximate {target construction} by {surrogate} with {dimensions}; explicitly list omitted components.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not label a hollow shell as filled and capped corking.

units.source_excerpt: For aluminum we use a thin shell with aluminum density and modulus and compare its exit-speed curve with the wooden bat.
units.function: Define the material scenario and common comparison output.
units.reusable_pattern: Define {material scenario} by {geometry and properties}; compare with {baseline} on {common metric} and matched constraints.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call a compound redesign a material-only effect.

units.source_excerpt: The trampoline effect involves exciting so-called hoop modes, or modes with an azimuthal dependence, which our model can not simulate directly.
units.function: Name the missing mechanism and why the core beam cannot represent it.
units.reusable_pattern: Mechanism {m} requires {degree of freedom}, which {current model} omits; treat the extension as exploratory.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim the omitted mode is captured by frequency alone.

units.source_excerpt: Instead we will artificially insert a hoop mode by hanging a mass from a spring from the spot of the bat the ball hits.
units.function: Declare the exploratory surrogate after rejecting the full shell solution as out of scope.
units.reusable_pattern: Because {full extension} is out of scope, use {surrogate} only to explore {mechanism}; state missing calibration parameters.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not interpret the surrogate quantitatively without modal mass and damping.

units.source_excerpt: The sweet spot depends on the local collision dynamics during a time too short for the entire bat and hands to respond rigidly.
units.function: Close the core mechanism with the collision-time interpretation.
units.reusable_pattern: The result follows from {local mechanism} acting over {time scale}, before {distant subsystem} can respond.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call simulated timing experimentally validated.

units.source_excerpt: The aluminum bat has a wider sweet region because waves travel and return more quickly than in wood in our modeled shells.
units.function: Tie the material comparison to wave-return timing and the modeled scope.
units.reusable_pattern: Scenario {A} produces {difference} relative to {B} because {mechanism}, conditional on {matched or unmatched design choices}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer league policy from an unmatched shell comparison.

units.source_excerpt: Our model does not include torsion, transverse shear, or a fully coupled hoop response.
units.function: Name the omitted physical mechanisms that bound the conclusions.
units.reusable_pattern: The model omits {mechanisms}; conclusions therefore apply only where {boundary condition} holds.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not present proposed mechanisms as implemented.

units.source_excerpt: Further experimental work on real wooden, corked, and aluminum bats is needed to test the numerical predictions.
units.function: End with the evidence required to validate the scenario comparisons.
units.reusable_pattern: Validate {predictions} using {matched systems}, measuring {outputs} under {controlled inputs}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim real-world confirmation before these tests.
